# Necessary Warning from the Author
## to the Reader of this book / from the
## 4th Chapter, Paragraph 43, of this treatise.

But Reader / I wish to have you faithfully warned / if you are not on the path of the prodigal / and returning-to-the-Father son <note>A reference to the Biblical parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15), which Böhme uses here as a metaphor for the soul turning away from worldly desires and back toward God.</note> / then leave this my book unread / otherwise it will go ill with you. For the Grand Prince Lucifer will not rest from troubling you. For in this book he stands before the children of God entirely naked and bare. He is ashamed of this, just like a person / who is made a laughingstock before all people for the sake of their misdeeds. Therefore be warned / if your <term>the<note>original: "dz," an early modern German abbreviation for "das."</note></term> tender flesh is too dear to you / then leave my book unread. If you do not follow this / and disaster arises for you / then I wish to be innocent / blame only yourself. For what I now recognize / that I write for myself as a <term>memorial<note>original: "Memorial." Here Böhme suggests his writing serves as a personal record or a spiritual aid for his own memory, rather than a standard textbook.</note></term> / but God well knows what He wishes to do / which is still to some extent hidden from me.

<image-desc>A decorative calligraphic horizontal flourish.</image-desc>

->J. B.<-

<summary>In this preface, Jacob Böhme warns that his work is spiritually volatile and should only be read by those truly seeking a return to God, as it exposes the nature of Lucifer. He frames the writing as a personal spiritual record and disclaims responsibility for any mental or spiritual distress it may cause the "unprepared" reader.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Böhme, spiritual warning, Lucifer, Prodigal Son, mystical insight, spiritual preparation, 17th-century theology</keywords>

### Hans Dieterich von Tschesch, in a missive 
### to H. P. V. H. dated Breslau 
### the 3rd of October, in the year 1641.

The philosophy and theology of Jacob Böhme is a most noble and deep foundation, universal, and extending into all things: but especially the teaching of the Three Principles <term>Three Principles|Böhme’s metaphysical system describing three realms: the dark fire-world of God's wrath, the light-world of God's love, and the physical world we inhabit</term>, which have their origin <note>original: "Uhrstandt," an archaic term for origin or primordial state</note> in the Holy Trinity / although the third principle must be properly distinguished.

I have closely examined the gift and teaching of this highly enlightened man / according to the gift that God has granted me / and found them entirely spiritual and well-distinguished / so that they are not only not offensive to any article of the Christian faith / but indeed explain them most excellently. And it is a light and a birth of this time / such as has hardly ever been opened before / explaining so precisely what God and Nature are. But just as it is a gift of God / so too is a gift of God required to recognize and understand that same light.

# PREFACE
## To the Christian, God-loving /
## Reader.

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap letter 'E' at the start of the first paragraph, intricately decorated with vines and scrolls in an oval frame.</image-desc>

From the 1. mother’s womb throughout the entire course of his time in this world, a person can undertake nothing more useful or necessary for himself than this: that he learns to know himself rightly: 1. What he is? 2. From what or from whom he originates? 3. For what purpose he was created? and 4. What his duty <note>original: "Ambt," referring to one's divinely appointed calling or office in life</note> is?

In such serious contemplation, he will initially 1 find how he, along with all creatures that exist, originates entirely from GOD. He will also find in all creatures 2 how he is the most noble creature among all created things. From this, he can well understand 3 how God is disposed toward him, since He made him lord over all creatures of this world, and endowed him above all creatures with sense, reason, and understanding—especially with speech—so that he can distinguish everything that makes a sound or stirs, moves, weaves <note>original: "webet," a term Böhme frequently uses to describe the pulsing, active movement of life and spirit within the universe</note>, and grows, and can judge the virtue, activity, and origin of each. And He has placed all of this into his hands, so that through his senses and reason he can master all such things, and use and direct them according to his will, as it pleases him.

Indeed, God has given 2. him an even higher and greater knowledge, so that he can look into the heart of all things to see what essence, power, and property <term>property|In Böhme’s thought, the "property" (Eigenschaft) of a thing is its specific spiritual quality or the way it manifests God's power</term> they have: whether it be in creatures, in the earth, in stones, in trees,

<margin>3.</margin> Above all this, God has given him understanding and the highest sensibility <note>original: "Sinnlichkeit," the capacity for perception and feeling</note>, so that he can recognize God his Creator—what, how, and who He may be? Also who he himself is? From what he was created and whence he came (meaning the human being), and how he is the image, essence, property, and child of the eternal, uncreated, and infinite God. How he was created out of God's essence, in which God has His own essence and property; in which He lives and reigns with His Spirit, through which God performs His works, and also loves him heartily as His own heart and essence. For whose sake He created this world along with all creatures, which for the most part could not live in such a state of being <term>state of being|original: "qualificirung," a term describing the interaction of qualities or the specific "flavor" of a thing's existence</term> without human reason and governance.

<margin>4.</margin> In this high contemplation stands Divine Wisdom <note>Often referred to as "Sophia" in this tradition, the mirror of God's glory</note> herself, and she has neither number nor end. And therein is recognized the Divine love toward man, so that man may recognize what GOD his Creator is: what He wishes to have done or left undone by him. And this is the most useful thing that man may ever fathom and seek in this world. For herein he learns to know himself—what kind of matter and essence he is, also from whence his sensibility and understanding originate, and how he was created out of God’s essence. Just as a mother gives birth to her child out of her own essence, and cares for it, and leaves all her goods to it as its own property, and makes it its possessor: thus God does with the human being, His child

# To the Christian Reader.

...child as well: He has created him and cares for him, and has made him the heir of all His goods.
<margin>Acts 17:28</margin>
In such contemplation, Divine knowledge and love toward God grow within the human being—just as between children and parents—so that the human being loves God his Father, because he recognizes that He is his Father, in whom he lives, moves, and has his being <note>The author quotes the Apostle Paul here, emphasizing the literal interconnectedness of God and humanity</note>, who cares for him and nourishes him. For thus speaks Christ, John 17:3, our brother, who was born of the Father for our salvation and sent into this world: "This is eternal life, that they might rightly recognize You, that You alone are the true GOD, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent."

<margin>5.</margin>
Since we now recognize ourselves—how we were created in God’s image, essence, and property <term>property|original: "Eigenthumb," implying both a possession and an inherent characteristic</term> out of God’s own essence—it is indeed fitting that we live in His obedience and follow Him, because He leads us as a father leads his children. We also have the promise that if we follow Him, we shall have the light of eternal life (John 8). Without this contemplation, we would all be blind and have no true knowledge of God, but would instead run along like dumb cattle, looking at ourselves and God's creation like a cow looks at a new barn door <note>A traditional German idiom (wie eine Kuh vor dem neuen Tor) describing a look of blank, uncomprehending astonishment</note>. We would set ourselves against God and His will, and live in opposition to the destruction of body and soul, and of God's noble creatures. Into such cruel and terrifying darkness we fall if we do not wish to learn to know ourselves: what we are, of what essence, and of what dignity? Whether we are eternal, or perishable with the body; or whether we must give an account <term>account|original: "Rechenschafft," a formal reckoning or audit</term> of our deeds and essence, since we were made masters of all creatures and created things, and have all of them in our power and governance.

# Preface

6. Since we then irrefutably see, know, and find that God will demand an accounting of all our deeds—how we have acted as stewards of His creatures—and since He punishes us terribly if we fall away from Him and His commandments: We have indeed seen terrifying examples of this throughout the history of the world, among Jews, Heathens, and Christians alike. We see this primarily in the example of the Great Flood, as well as in Sodom and Gomorrah; also with Pharaoh and the host of Israel in the desert, and thereafter evermore up to the present day <note>original: "biß auff dato"</note>. Thus, it is most necessary that we learn wisdom and learn to recognize ourselves—to see what great vices we carry within us and what horrible wolves <note>A metaphor for predatory sins or destructive impulses that reside within the human heart</note> are among us to resist God and His will.

7. For no human being can excuse themselves through ignorance, since God’s will is written into our very minds <term>minds|original: "Gemühte," referring to the seat of emotions, will, and conscience</term>, so that we well know what we ought to do. All of creation also bears witness against us; furthermore, we have God’s Law and Commandment, so that there is no excuse other than our own sleepy, lazy negligence. Thus, we are found to be lazy, useless servants in the Lord’s vineyard <note>A reference to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard from Matthew 20</note>.

8. Finally, it is of the highest necessity for us that we learn to know ourselves because the Devil dwells with us in this world. He is God’s enemy and ours, who daily seduces and deceives us into falling away from God our Father, just as he did to our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note>, so that he may increase his kingdom and deprive us of our eternal salvation; as it stands written in 1 Peter 5, verse 8:
> Your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.

9. Because we are indeed hovering in such terrifying danger in this world—surrounded by enemies on all sides and walking quite insecurely...

<summary>The author argues that self-knowledge is a moral necessity to avoid divine punishment and the deceptions of the Devil, who seeks to lead humanity away from God. He cites biblical precedents like the Great Flood and the Fall of Man as warnings against spiritual negligence.</summary>
<keywords>accountability, stewardship, Great Flood, self-knowledge, spiritual warfare, the Devil, 1 Peter 5:8, conscience</keywords>

->### To the Christian Reader.<-

[we] have in our pilgrimage <note>The "pilgrimage" refers to the traditional Christian view of earthly life as a temporary journey toward heaven</note>, and moreover carry the worst enemy within us, whom we cover up and do not wish to get to know. Yet he is the most harmful guest, who plunges us into God’s wrath: Yes, he is himself the wrath of GOD, who plunges us into the eternal fire of wrath, into eternal, unquenchable pain. It is therefore very necessary that we learn to know this same enemy well—what he is, who he is, and how he is; how he enters into us, what his rights and property within us are, as well as the Devil's right and access to us. We must know how he is befriended by our own enemy who dwells within us: how they are favorable and kind to one another, how they are both enemies of God, and how they always lie in wait for us to destroy and murder us.

<margin>10.</margin>
Furthermore, it is highly necessary for us to consider and to learn to know ourselves for these great reasons: because we see and know that because of our own enemy (who is God's enemy and ours, who dwells within us, indeed who is half of who we are <note>Refers to the "Old Adam" or the corrupt part of human nature that theologians argued must be overcome</note>), we must die and decay. If this enemy becomes powerful within us, so that he gains the upper hand and becomes the master <note>original: "Primus," meaning the first or chief</note>, he plunges us into the abyss to be with all the devils. There we would dwell forever in eternal, unquenchable torment and pain in eternal darkness. Yes, he plunges us into a house of desolation, into the eternal forgetting of all good, and into God’s aversion, so that God and all creatures become our eternal enemies.

<margin>11.</margin>
We have an even higher reason to learn to know ourselves—how we are in both good and evil—because we have the promise of eternal life. If we overcome our own enemy, along with the Devil, we shall be God's children. we shall live in His kingdom with Him, and in Him among His holy angels

From where or through what has evil come into the Devil and humans, as well as into all creatures? Since the Devil was a holy angel, and man was also created good, yet such discord is found in all creatures that everything bites, strikes, pushes, crushes, and is hostile to each other; and thus there is a resistance <note>original: "Wiederwille"—literally "against-will," describing a state of opposition, contrariety, or repulsion between forces</note> in all creatures, and so every body is at odds with itself. This is seen not only in living creatures, but also in the stars, elements, earth, stones, metals, leaves, grass, and wood; in all of them there is poison and malice. It is found that it must be so, for otherwise there would be no life nor mobility, nor would there be color, virtue <note>original: "Tugend"—here used in the archaic sense of an inherent power or medicinal property</note>, density or thinness, or any kind of sensation; rather, everything would be a nothingness.

<margin>14.</margin>
In such high contemplation, one finds that all of this comes from and out of God Himself, and that it is of His own essence—which He is Himself—and that He has created it thus out of Himself. Does the evil belong to formation and mobility, and the good to love, and the harsh or resistant to joy? As long as the creature is in the light of God, the wrathful or resistant element creates a rising eternal joy; but if the light of God is extinguished, it becomes an eternal rising painful torment and the hellish fire.

<margin>15.</margin>

<margin>John 4:24.</margin>
Since God has now created this world along with everything in it, He had no other material from which to make it than His own essence, out of Himself. Now God is a Spirit who is incomprehensible, having neither beginning nor end, and His greatness and depth are everything.

A Spirit, however, does nothing but ascend, flow, move, and forever give birth to itself; and primarily has three forms within its birth: namely 1. **Bitter**, 2. **Harsh**, 3. and **Heat**. And yet, these three forms are not a first, second, or third; rather, all three are only one, and each gives birth to the second and third. For between the Harsh and the Bitter, the **Fire** is born, and the fierceness of the fire is the Bitterness, or the sting itself; and the Harshness is the source-stock, the father of both, and yet is also born from them. For a spirit is like a will or mind that ascends, and in its ascending, it remains, <term>infects</term> <note>original: "inficiret"—in this context, it means to permeate, influence, or spiritually impregnate.</note>, or gives birth to itself.

5. For one cannot say that in God there is Fire, Bitterness, or Harshness—much less Air, Water, or Earth—only one sees that these have come from Him. <margin>9.</margin>

In this severe drawing-together, Bitterness arises; for in the severe contraction, the spirit sharpens itself so that it becomes quite anxious. Take an example in man: when he becomes angry, see how his spirit draws itself inward, which makes him bitterly tremble. If this is not quickly resisted and extinguished, the fire of wrath will ignite within him so that he burns in malice. Then, in the spirit and the mind, a substance or a whole essence of vengeance will immediately take shape.

### More Concerning the Birth.

<margin>9.</margin>The birth of eternal nature is just like the senses in man / where a sense is born from something / and afterwards spreads into infinity. Or like the root of a tree is born / and thereafter from it the trunk and many branches and twigs / also many roots from that single root / and many branches and twigs; and it all comes from the first single root. # Of the Three Principles

### Chapter 3

The source-spirits <note>original: "Quell-geiste"; Böhme's term for the active, flowing forces or "qualities" of divine nature</note> are but a single center, wherein the fire-source rises up, and from the fire-flash comes the light; and in every source there are the first six-fold forms.

<margin>11.</margin> But mark the depth in this parable: I posit this: The harsh source in the original ground <note>original: "uhrkunde"; referring to the primal state or the "Ur-ground" of existence before manifest light</note> is the mother, out of which the other five sources—namely Bitter, Fire, Love, Tone, and Water—are born. Now these are members in their birth, and without them she [the mother] would also be nothing but an anxious, dark valley, where there would be no mobility, nor any light or life. But now that life is born within her through the igniting of the light, she rejoices in her own quality, and works upward in her own harsh quality within life; there a center then opens up again, and life is born out of her once more in a six-fold form—but now no longer in such anxiety as in the original ground, but in great joy.

<margin>12.</margin> For the source of great anxiety, which in the original ground resided in harshness before the light—and from which the bitter sting was born—is now transformed into the gentle source of love in the light from the water-spirit. And from bitterness and the sting, the source and rising of joy in the light has now come to be. Thus the fire-flash is henceforth the father of the light, and the light shines within it, and is now the sole cause of the moving birth. And the birth of love, which in the original ground was the anxious source, is now *Sul* <note>likely a reference to "Sulphur," which Böhme associates with the "soul" or the flammable principle that hosts the light</note> or the *Oleum* <note>Latin: "oil"</note>, the friendly source that penetrates through all sources, from which or out of which the light is kindled.

# Of the Three Principles

<margin>Chapter 4</margin> **Where does evil come from?** Since He alone is the Life and the Light, and the holy Power—as it is undeniably true—from where, then, does the **Wrath of God** <note>original: *Zorn Gottes*. Where do the Devil and his will come from, as well as the fire of Hell? From what do they take their origin? Since nothing existed before the times of the world except God alone, and He was and is a Spirit and remains so for eternity: from what was the **first matter** <note>original: *erſte materi*</note> for wickedness made? <margin>35.</margin> What, then, moved the Devil to become angry and evil? What is the **first matter** <note>original: *materia*</note> within him, since he was created out of the most original, eternal Spirit? <margin>36.</margin> At this point, dear reader, open the eyes of your mind! Know that no other torment will torture him but his own torment within himself. <margin>62.</margin>

A difficult term in Böhme's lexicon referring to the original "evidence" or the way the hidden God makes Himself perceptible and known.</term>. I write solely to the end that man might learn to know himself—what he is, what God, Heaven, Angels, Devils, and Hell are, as well as the **Wrath of God** and hellish fire. For I am permitted to write this far from the source of manifestation <note>original: *Uhrkundt*.</note>.

<margin>63.</margin>

The primordial "dark" quality of God's power when it is not tempered by the Light of the Son.</note>, in the valley of darkness, and your noble image [derived] from God will become a serpent and a dragon.

# Chapter VI.

## Of the Separation in the Creation in the Third Principle.

1. If one now investigates the separation and the outgoing in the **Third Principle** <term>Third Principle: Böhme’s term for our visible, material world, which exists as a manifestation of the interplay between the spiritual realms of Light and Darkness.</term> of this world—how the starry heaven arose, and how every star has a particular property and form within itself, since in each a particular center is noted, so that each is fixed and a master for itself, and each rules in the **Matrix** <term>Matrix: Latin for "womb"; the generative, shaping power of nature.</term> of this world, acting upon and giving birth in the Matrix according to its kind. And look thereafter at the Sun, which is their king, heart, and life, without whose light and power they all would accomplish no effect, but would stand in hard, dark death, and in this world everything would be a nothing—everything would be only a fierce, rough harshness <note>original: "Herbigkeit" — in Böhme's philosophy, this is the first quality of nature: a cold, contracting, and astringent force.</note>. And look further at the **Elements**: Fire, Air, and Water—how they always give birth to one another, one within the other, and then how the stars rule in these as in their own property <note>original: "Engenthumb" — domain or rightful possession.</note>. And look at the Mother from whom all this essence goes out. Thus we come to the separation and to the **Eternal Mother**, the bearer of all things.

<margin>1. Deuteronomy 30:14.</margin>
As was mentioned at the beginning of the previous chapter, it is nothing strange if a person speaks, writes, and teaches about the creation of the world, even though they were not present there, provided they possess the true knowledge in the spirit. For there, as if in a mirror, one sees all things in the Mother of the Birth-Giver <note>original: "Mutter der Gebährerin"; in Böhme's thought, this refers to the primordial matrix or the creative womb of nature from which all existence is generated.</note>; for one thing always lies within another, and the more one searches, the more one finds. <margin>2. Genesis 1:31.</margin>

<margin>8.</margin> On the second day, **God** created the firmament of heaven—the strong enclosure between the darkness of the most original *matrix* <term>Matrix: Latin for "womb"; Böhme uses it to describe the primal, creative environment from which all matter is born.</term>—so that it would not ignite anymore and produce earth and stones. Therefore, He made the enclosure, or firmament, out of the midst of the water, which resists the fire-power; and it became the visible heaven, out of which the creatures have come, and from which the elements—**fire**, air, and water—now proceed.

<margin>9.</margin> On the third day, **GOD** divided the waters on earth through the *Fiat* <note>original: "Fiat"; Latin for "Let there be," the divine command of creation.</note> and brought them to special places, so that it might be a delight on earth, and that the earth became dry. There, life turned green through death, and there arose grass and herbs and all kinds of trees and all kinds of plants, each according to the eternal source, just as it had been before. For no Doctors <note>In the 17th century, a "Doctor" was the highest academic rank in theology; Böhme is contrasting formal university education with direct spiritual wisdom.</note> are found on this path in this school, but only sheer pupils.

<margin>10.</margin>
Therefore, Master Hans <note>original: "Meister Hans"; a derogatory nickname Böhme often uses for self-important scholars or clergymen who rely on book-learning rather than the Holy Spirit.</note> in his crowned little hut <note>A mocking reference to the academic cap or perhaps the narrow, sheltered environment of institutional theology.</note> must not think himself so clever in these matters, nor pour out his mockery so boldly. For he knows nothing as long as he is a mocker: Let his little hut not suit him so well, nor let him boast of his human calling <note>original: "Ruff"; referring to a professional appointment or ecclesiastical title.</note>, claiming he sits in his office by Divine ordinance, when he is actually seated there not by God, but by human favor <note>original: "Menschen-gunst"; referring to positions obtained through political or social connections rather than spiritual merit.</note>. Let him not forbid the path to Paradise too much; he does not know it himself, and he will have to give a heavy account of his sitting there through human favor while he boasts of a Divine calling. Since the Spirit of God is far from him, he becomes a liar and lies against the Godhead.

### The Gates

<margin>18.</margin>
**P**aradise stands in the Divine Power, and is nothing bodily or tangible <note>meaning: it cannot be grasped by physical hands or the five senses.</note>; rather, its bodiliness or tangibility is like that of the Angels, where there is a bright, visible Essence, just as if it were material—and it is indeed material, but formed purely out of the Power, where everything is transparent and shining. In this state, the center of birth <note>Böhme’s term for the dynamic process of God constantly "generating" or "birthing" reality.</note> is within all things; therefore, this birth is without end or number.

<margin>19.</margin>
I give you a likeness in the human mind, out of which thoughts are born, of which there is neither end nor number. For every thought has the power to give birth to other thoughts within its center. In this same way, Paradise is from eternity to eternity. Because the Light of God is eternal and shines without wavering or lack, there is also an unchanging Essence within this birth, where everything rises up in pure perfection in great love.

<margin>20.</margin>
For the Spirit of Knowledge <note>original: "Erkäntnuß"; refers to experiential spiritual insight.</note> grants us this: that in Paradise there are growths <note>plants or vegetation</note> just as in this world, and in such forms, but not with such a harsh source <note>original: "quell"; refers to the underlying quality or "taste" of a thing's nature.</note> or tangibility. For the material or body <note>original: "Corpus"</note> is Power and Essence in the heavenly **substance** <term>Limbus: Böhme’s term for the holy, spiritual "earth" or the extract of the divine world from which the soul is formed.</term>. The root stands in the **womb** <term>Matrix: The divine "mother" or the receptive, generative principle from which all forms emerge.</term>, in which there is neither earth nor stones, for it is another **principle** <term>Principium: One of Böhme's three fundamental realms of existence (Darkness, Light, and the Physical world).</term>. The fire within it is God the Father; and the light within it is God the Son; and the air within it is God the Holy Spirit; and the power from which everything arises is Heaven and Paradise.

# Divine Essence

<margin>Chapter 10</margin>
...God himself? Therein lies the purpose, the ground, and the knowledge. See, if the **will** <note>original: *Wille*</note> were in only one single essence, then the **mind** <note>original: *Gemüte*—Böhme’s term for the seat of the soul's thoughts and emotions</note> would also have only one quality to provide for the will, and it would be an unmovable thing that always lay still, doing nothing more than one single thing. In such a state, there would be no joy, no knowledge, no art, no science of more things, and there would be no wisdom. Furthermore, if that quality did not exist within the infinite, then everything would be a nothingness; there would be no mind or will toward anything, for there would be only the One.

<margin>36.</margin>
Thus, one cannot say that the whole of God, with all **three principles** <note>Böhme’s framework: 1. The dark fire-source (the Father), 2. The light-world (the Son), and 3. The outward world of nature (the Holy Spirit/manifestation)</note>, exists within a single will and essence; there is a distinction. Even though the first and third principles are not called **God** <margin>GOD.</margin>—and indeed are not God—they are nonetheless His essence, from which God's **Light** and **Heart** <note>The "Heart" refers to the Second Person of the Trinity, or Christ, the center of divine love</note> are eternally born. It is one being, much like the body and soul in a human being.

<margin>37.
1. Eternal Mind.
2. Eternal Will.
3. Eternal Heart of God.
4. Light.
5. Power.
6. Spirit.
7. Almighty God.</margin>
If the eternal **mind** did not exist, from which the eternal **will** proceeds, there would be no God. But as it is, the eternal mind exists; it gives birth to the eternal will, and the eternal will gives birth to the eternal **Heart of God**. The Heart gives birth to the **Light**, and the Light to the **Power** <note>original: *Krafft*—the active, virtuous energy of the divine</note>, and the Power to the **Spirit**, and that is the **Almighty GOD**, who exists in an unchangeable will. For if the mind no longer gave birth to the will, then the will would not give birth to the Heart, and everything would be a nothingness. But since the mind gives birth to the will, and the will the Heart, and the Heart the Light, and the Light the Power, and the Power the Spirit, the Spirit now gives birth back to the mind; for the Spirit possesses the power, and the power is the Heart, and it is an unbreakable bond.

<summary>Böhme explains that God is not a static unity but a dynamic process of eternal generation. He details how the "Almighty God" emerges through a circular chain of Mind, Will, Heart, Light, Power, and Spirit, forming an unbreakable divine bond.</summary>

# Of the Three Principles

<margin>Chapter 2.
7+</margin>
Now it is clearly evident to us that the paradisiacal fruit, which was good, was not entirely earthly; for as Moses himself says, there were two kinds: one good to eat and pleasant to look upon, and in the other lay death and fragility <note>original: *Zerbrechlichkeit*—referring to the tendency of material things to decay or break apart</note>. In the paradisiacal fruit there was no death and no fragility. But if death had been in it, then Adam would have eaten death in every fruit. Yet since no death was in it, the fruit could not be entirely earthly; although it grew out of the earth, the power of God (of the second **Principle** <term>The "Second Principle" in Böhme's philosophy represents the world of Divine Light and love</term>) was infused within it. It truly grew from the earth in the third **Principle** <term>The "Third Principle" represents the physical, material world we inhabit</term>, which God cursed after the earthly eating, so that no more paradisiacal fruit grew from the earth.

<margin>8.</margin>
Furthermore, if Adam were meant to eat earthly fruit, he would have had to eat into a body and possess intestines; then such a stench, which we now carry in our bodies, would have existed in Paradise within God’s holiness. Additionally, by eating earthly food, he would have consumed the fruit of the stars and elements, which would have immediately interacted <term>original: *inqualiret*—a term Böhme uses to describe how different qualities or forces "work into" or influence one another</term> within him, just as happened after the Fall. Also, his progeny would have grown to be like all the animals; for the animal essence <note>original: *thierische Essentia*</note> would have immediately equaled the human in power, and one stronger individual would have ruled over the others.

<margin>9+</margin>
Therefore, Adam's form was of an entirely different nature: He was a heavenly and paradisiacal man, and he was meant to eat from heavenly and paradisiacal fruit, and in that same power rule over all animals, as well as the stars and elements. Neither cold nor heat was meant to touch him; otherwise, God would have created a rough hide for him, just like all the animals, and not left him so naked.

### Of the Kingdom of Christ in this World.

39. **B**ecause man had then truly entered this world in the spirit, and now possessed all the gates within—such as the kingdom of heaven, as well as the kingdom of hell and also the kingdom of this world—he therefore had to live in the "press" <note>original: "quätsche" — a crushing squeeze or pressure between two opposing forces</note> between heaven and this world. There, the devil awakened one mocker after another, who raised up the kingdom of wrath <term>Grimmigkeit</term> <note>A central term in Böhme’s thought, referring to the harsh, fire-like, and vengeful aspect of nature when it is not tempered by divine light and love.</note> and constantly stirred up conflict against the children of God. Thus the world became full of tyrants, as well as bestial violators of blood, murderers, and thieves, because greed had grown. Therefore, the office of the ruler was most useful, so that it might restrain the godless oppressor with force.

40. And one sees how Divine Providence <term>Fürsichtigkeit</term> itself comes to the aid of the kingdom of this world, and through the spirit of this world awakens rulers who carried out punishment. But the Spirit of God complains about them, that they have become tyrants who suppressed everything under them with force. And now Abel’s church <note>In Böhme’s typology, Abel represents the true, humble, and spiritual believer, whereas Cain represents the worldly and institutionalized power.</note> would not consist therein in love, but rather the strong power of God was used to suppress the evildoer.

41. Indeed, the judges and kings, as well as princes and governors, are God's officials in the house of this world, whom God has appointed because of sin, so that they should "cut sharply" <note>meaning to exercise strict justice or the power of the sword</note> so that the oppressor of the godless might be restrained.

42. And their station is founded in the original source <term>Uhrkundt</term> <note>Böhme uses this term to refer to the fundamental "original record" or essential foundation of all existence.</note> of beings, for in the beginning God created the thrones according to His eternal wisdom; just as there are throne-princes in heaven, so also there are such in hell, and thus in regions according to the seven spirits of eternal nature.

The physical world</term>. # Of the Divine Essence

<margin>Chapter 22</margin>
...[the earthly] element does not grasp [the divine], just as little as the body grasps the soul. Likewise, *Christ* truly took our human essences <term>essences: the fundamental properties or "substance" of human nature</term> upon himself in the body of the Virgin *Mary* and became our brother. Yet these human essences cannot grasp his eternal Godhead; only the new man born in God grasps the Godhead, in the same way that the body relates to the soul, and in no other way.

<margin>42.</margin>
Therefore, the body of *Christ* is beneath the Godhead, and within these our human essences, he suffered death. His Godhead went into death in the midst of the holy man within the pure element <note>The "pure element" refers to the spiritual world or the "quintessence" that exists behind the four physical elements.</note>, and took away death’s power. He separated the natural soul—which *Christ* commended to his Father as he died on the Cross—from the kingdom of this world, as well as from death, the devil, and hell, through his mighty Divine power. He opened a gate for all of us who come to him and claim him as our own with our senses and minds. In this way, the Father draws our soul, which is in him, into the pure love of *Christ*. There, the soul sets its imagination <term>imagination: in Böhme’s thought, this refers to the soul’s power of focus and desire that shapes its inner reality</term> once again through *Christ* into the Holy Trinity. It is then fed by the Word of the Lord <note>original: "Verbo Domini"</note>, where it becomes an angel once again, purely separated from the kingdom of the devil and this world through the death of *Christ*.

<margin>43.</margin>

It was not at all for the sake of the animal body, which must melt back into the four elements and become nothing; of which nothing remains but the shadow in the figure of all the works and beings that it ever made.

In Böhme's cosmology, this refers to the spiritual and physical influence of the stars and planets upon the world.</note>, and also in the Element; and the Son, His Heart, is the Sun, who places the entire constellation into a light, sweet delight; and the Holy Spirit is the air of life, without which no Sun or constellation could exist; and the combined spirit of the *Greater World* <note>original: "Majoris Mundi," referring to the macrocosm or the universe as a whole.</note> is the chaste Virgin <note>Böhme frequently identifies the "Virgin" with Sophia, or Divine Wisdom, who acts as a mirror or mediator for God's glory.</note> before God, which spirit of the *Greater World* gives to all creatures in this world their mind, sense, and understanding through the influence of the stars; and likewise so in heaven.

<margin>62.</margin>
The earthly earth compares itself to the *Holy Ternary* <note>original: "Ternario Sancto." This term refers to the manifestation of the Trinity in a "holy substance" or "holy earth," which Böhme distinguishes from the heavy, fallen earth we inhabit.</note>, within which is the heavenly *Aquaster* <note>original: "Aquaster," a term borrowed from Paracelsus meaning a spiritual, celestial water or vital fluid.</note>—understand [this to be] in the heavenly earth, which I call the Element, which is pure there. Thus God is a spirit, and the pure Element is heavenly earth, for it is substantial; and the essences in the heavenly earth are the Paradise of growth; and the Virgin of Wisdom is to be compared thus to the great spirit of the entire heavenly world; and she reveals the great wonders not only in the heavenly earth, but also in the entire depth of the Godhead.

<margin>63.</margin>
For the Godhead is incomprehensible and invisible, yet perceptible; but the Virgin is visible as a pure spirit, and the Element is her body; this is called the *Holy Ternary* <note>original: "Ternarius Sanctus"</note>, the holy earth.

And into this *Holy Ternary* the invisible Godhead has entered, so that it may be an eternal marriage; so that, to speak in an analogy, the Godhead is in the pure Element, and the Element is the Godhead. For God and the *Holy Ternary* have become one thing—not in spirit, but in essence—just like body and soul; and as the soul is over the body, so also is God over the *Holy Ternary*.

Your faith is its faith, and your confidence in the covenant with God is its confidence; for they are indeed your <term>essences</term> <note>original: "Essentien"; in Böhme’s thought, these are the fundamental spiritual "substances" or qualities that pass from parent to child.</note>, and are born of your soul. <margin>33.</margin> You should not, however, neglect baptism for that reason. For as soon as the child is born into the world, it is separated from its tree and is in this world; there it must enter the covenant for itself, and you, with your faith, must present it, and with your prayer deliver it into God’s covenant. No pomp is required for this—by which the covenant is only dishonored—for this is a matter of great earnestness.

<margin>34.</margin> There are three witnesses to this covenant: One is called God the Father, the second God the Son, and the third God the Holy Spirit. These are the master-craftsmen who perform the office, who do the baptizing. Like a sow before a mirror?

48. When it [the soul] departs from the <term>Testament of Christ</term> <note>Referring to the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper.</note>, it enters again into the stall of robbery and is a murderer. It howls with the dogs; it is a perjured harlot. When it departs from the Covenant, it goes into the harlot's corner; there one looks on and pretends to great holiness, saying: "Oh, today is a holy day for me, I must not sin," yet it thinks, "tomorrow or the day after you want to go back there again."

49. O you rogue, just stay away from Christ's Testament unless you bring another man <note>Böhme refers to the "new man" or the reborn spiritual nature that must accompany the physical person to the sacrament.</note> to it; you are only a murderer and offend your neighbor as long as you are on such a path. Your prayer is false; it does not come from the bottom of your heart. Your heart desires only the pleasure of this world, and the <term>driver</term> <note>original: "Treiber." This is Böhme's term for the spirit of the world or the dark principle (sometimes associated with the devil) that "drives" or compels the unregenerate soul.</note> receives your prayer; he is your god; therefore, think on what you do.

50. O <term>Babel</term> <note>Böhme uses this biblical name to represent the institutionalized, divided, and hypocritical church systems of his day.</note>, we would have much to say to you, but not here. One will speak with you in wrath, at which the <term>elements</term> <note>original: "Elementa." This refers to the basic constituents of the physical world.</note> shall tremble; go out, it is time for the wrath to subside.

# A Beautiful Mirror for All Hungry, Penitent Souls.
<margin>Chapter 24.</margin>

<margin>1.</margin>
My dear reader! We declare this to you: that all things, proceeding from the <term>original source</term> <note>original: "Uhrkunde." Böhme uses this term to describe the primordial origin or "primal record" of all being.</note> of the <term>Essence of all essences</term> <note>original: "Wesen aller Wesen." A common Böhmean term for the Ground of all being or the Godhead.</note>, each have their impulse in their own form according to their origin; and that thing always creates the same essence with which the spirit is pregnant. The body must always work within that in which the spirit is kindled. When I reflect and consider why I write in this way, rather than leaving it to other clever and sharp-minded people, I find that my spirit is kindled in this essence about which I write. For there is a living, running fire of these things in my spirit. Therefore, whatever else I undertake, this matter always wells up from within, and thus I am captured by it in my spirit; it is laid upon me as a work that I must perform. Since it is then my work, which my spirit pursues, I will write it down as a <term>Memorial</term> <note>A remembrance or written record intended to preserve a spiritual experience for the future.</note> for myself—and in exactly such a manner as I recognize it in my spirit, and in the way I came to it. I will set down nothing foreign, nothing that I have not experienced myself, so that I may not be found a liar before God.

<margin>2.</margin>
If it should happen that someone desires to follow after me and craves the knowledge of these things about which I write, I give him this advice: that he should follow me in the <term>Table of Succession</term> <note>original: "Nachfolge-Taffel." This refers to the progression of Böhme's arguments or the spiritual path he maps out in the text.</note>, not immediately with the pen, but rather with the labor of the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "Gemüht." In Böhme's terminology, the *Gemüht* is the seat of the soul's desires, will, and emotional disposition; it is the "inner man."</note>. Then he will experience how I have been able to write thus, even though I have not been taught by the schools of this world—except only a very little—with this meager <term>handwriting</term> <note>original: "Handschrifft." Böhme refers to his own lack of formal academic training, identifying himself as a simple craftsman rather than a scholar.</note> which is before your eyes.

O, if only the Physician would come to bind us up so that our soul might become living again, how we would rejoice! Such is the aim of Desire, and it has its longing wish. And although the Physician is there, the Mind can nowhere grasp Him, for it is too severely wounded and lies half dead.

<margin>5.</margin> My dear Mind, you think you are quite healthy, but you are so severely beaten that you no longer feel your sickness; yet you are subjected very nearly unto death. How then can you consider yourself healthy?

Ah, my dear soul, do not boast of your health; you lie captured in heavy bonds.

In Böhme’s cosmology, man is composed of three parts: the eternal soul, the "sidereal" spirit (astrological/mental influence), and the physical body of elements. The sidereal spirit is what drives natural impulses.</note> in man. The soul says: "It is not right." Then the body says: "We must have these things, so that we may live and have enough." Thus it goes on, all mixed together, and a **true Christian** does not even know himself; how then should he be recognized by others? The Devil can easily hide him so that he is not recognized. And this is his **masterpiece** <note>original: *Meister-stück*. Böhme often portrays the Devil as a cunning craftsman of spiritual deception.</note>, when he can lead a true Christian into vice, so that he falls into sin; so that from the outside nothing is recognized in him except that he rebukes others for their sins, yet sins himself outwardly.

<margin>35.</margin>
And if he now sins, it is not he who does it in the **new man** <note>original: *neuen Menschen*. A Pauline concept referring to the spiritually reborn nature of a believer.</note>, but the **old man** <note>original: *Alte*. Referring to the "Old Adam" or the fallen, unregenerate nature.</note> in sin, who is subject to sin; who is in **God's wrath** <note>original: *Gottes Zorne*. In Böhme's system, "Wrath" is the dark, fiery foundational principle of nature that remains harsh until it is transformed by the Light of Love.</note>; the wrath drives him so that he does not always do right. And if he does something good, he does it not of his own will and powers, but the **new man** compels him to it, so that he must do it; for the old is fragile <note>original: *zerbrechlich*. This carries the sense of being perishable or prone to breaking under the weight of sin.</note>, but the soul is indestructible. Therefore the poor soul stands always in conflict, and is caught **between the door and the hinge** <note>original: *zwischen Thür und Angel*. A German idiom meaning to be in a tight spot or caught in a painful squeeze.</note>, and must certainly let itself be squeezed.

<margin>36.</margin>
We do not say that sin in the old man does no harm for that reason, even if the new man cannot always restrain it; for it still gives offense, and we should live to God out of the new man, even though it is not possible to be perfect in this world; yet we must always persevere. And the new man is in a field, where the field is cold, bitter, fierce, and frozen.

<margin>37.</margin>
And just as the plant grows out of the earth from a lovely sunshine; so also our new man **in Christ** <note>original: *in Christo*.</note> [grows] out of the old, fierce, cold, rough man of our earthly flesh...

### Chapter 25. Mobility, the Kingdom, Power and Glory

<margin><insert>Handwritten flourish</insert></margin> Therefore we have often said that the Wrath <note>In Böhme’s thought, "Zorn" (Wrath) is not just anger, but the raw, dark fire of existence that provides the "root" or energy for life; without the Light of God, it is hellish, but with the Light, it becomes the "fire" of love.</note> is a root of life; and if it is without Light, then it is not God, but Hellish Fire; but if the Light shines within it, it becomes Paradise and full of joy.

<margin>71.</margin> Thus we can say nothing else of Christ’s soul, but that when he commended it into the Father’s hands, the Father took it into his Divine Power. Understand: it previously stood therein with its own root, but its own root was without God’s Light, in wrath <note>Böhme refers here to the human soul's natural state apart from grace.</note>. Now Christ’s soul came into God’s Light within the wrath; then the devils trembled, for the Light took the wrath captive, and the wrath became Paradise in the Kingdom of Heaven—understand, His wrath—and in Hell, wrath remained. For the Light shut the Principle <note>The "Three Principles" are Böhme's framework for reality: 1) The dark fire/wrath, 2) The light/love of God, and 3) The external physical world.</note> of Hell, to be understood thus: that no devil may look into it; he is blind within it, and it is his terror and shame.

<margin>72+</margin> Thus you should not think that Christ’s soul traveled far away from the body; for were not all three Principles on the Cross? Why then not also in the Grave? The moment Christ released the kingdom of this world from himself, Christ’s soul broke into Death and into the Wrath of God; and in that same moment, the Wrath was reconciled to Love in the Light, and it became Paradise; and the devils were captured within themselves in the Wrath along with all godless souls. And immediately life blossomed through death; there death was broken and became a mockery. To the godless, who remained in the Wrath, it is a death; but to the Saints in Christ, it is a Life.

<margin>73+</margin> Thus the soul of Christ rested forty hours in the Grave in the Father, present with its body.

### Of Christ’s Ascension.

98. 100. Now Reason speaks: Where has Christ gone? Has he gone out of this world, high above the stars into another heaven? Hear, my dear Reason, incline your mind toward Christ, and see; I will tell you, for we see and know it—not I. For when I speak as "We," you must not understand merely my earthly humanity; for the Spirit that drives this pen is also named with me: Therefore I write and say, when I wish to speak of myself as the author, "We." For I knew nothing, if the Spirit had not breathed knowledge into me; and it could not have been found in any other way, for the Spirit did not wish it otherwise, but rather hid itself until my soul showed itself quite restless within me with great longing for the Spirit, until I learned what it was.

Even the devil, who dwells in this same place but within the first principle <note>The "first principle" is the dark, fiery source of strength and wrath that exists behind all manifestation.</note>, is a prisoner of our Christ.

You must understand how everything has the nature of a creature <note>original: "Creatürlich"; meaning everything has a defined, created form and limit.</note>: His love and His wrath alike. There is only one birth <note>original: "Gebuhrt"; Böhme uses this to mean the process by which reality is continuously generated or "born."</note>, as was mentioned before. The distinction is such that one cannot say the devils live far away from Christ. No, they are near, but they are not reached by eternity. For they cannot see the clear Godhead in the light, but are blinded by it. In the same way, we would never see or feel them in eternity—just as we do not see them now—because they are in a different principle. Thus, that principle remains separate.

<margin>106.</margin>
Therefore, my dear soul <note>original: "Gemühte"; refers to the mind, spirit, or inner disposition of the reader.</note>, know that the creature of Christ is the center <note>original: "Centrum"</note> of this throne, from which all life (meaning heavenly life) goes out. For the Holy Trinity is in that center—and not only in that center, but in all angelic thrones, and also in the holy souls of human beings. We must speak in this way only so that you may understand.

So the body—meaning the creature, the man Christ—is seated in the midst of this throne. He stands thus in heaven (meaning in His own principle), sitting with His throne at the right hand of God the Father.

How you will rejoice in the Lord!

<margin>4.</margin>
The Last Judgment is regarded in this way: just as we know how all things took their beginning, so shall they also have their end. For before the times of the world, there was nothing but the eternal band <term>Bande; the fundamental spiritual connection or knot of divine properties that precedes physical existence</term>, which made itself; and in the band was the Spirit, and the Spirit was in God, who is the highest Good, who ever was from eternity and never took a beginning. But this world has a beginning out of the eternal band within time.

<margin>5.</margin>
For this world creates a time; therefore it must pass away. And just as it was once a "nothing," so it will become a "nothing" again. For the Spirit hovered in the ether <note>original: "Æther"; the subtle spiritual atmosphere or heavenly element</note>, and within it was born the Limbo <note>original: "Limbus"; in Böhme’s thought, this refers to the transitional, formative substance or "chaos" from which physical matter was shaped</note>, which is transitory, and out of which all things come. At that time, there was no carver <note>original: "Schnizer"; a craftsman or sculptor</note> other than the Spirit in the essences <note>original: "Essentien"</note>, or the Vulcan <term>Vulcanus; a term borrowed from alchemy referring to the inner "fire-artist" or natural force that shapes and refines matter</term>. Furthermore, there were no essences unless they were born in the will of the Spirit; therein is the carver, who has carved all things out of nothing—simply out of the will. Since it is then carved out of the eternal will, it is eternal—not in its outward substance <note>original: "Wesen"</note>, but in the will. And after the breaking of the substance, this world stands entirely in the will, as a figure <note>original: "Figur"; a symbolic representation or permanent spiritual pattern</note> of God’s wondrous deeds.

<margin>6.</margin>
Thus we know that where a will exists, it must grasp itself so that it is a will; and this grasping creates an attraction, and that which is attracted is in the will,

9. So let everyone see to it how they use their reason, so that they may stand in great honor within the wonders of God.

<margin>Nature-fire.</margin> We know that this world shall perish in fire—and not a fire of wood or herb, for that would not turn a stone to ash or make it into nothing. Nor will any fire be piled up into which this world should be thrown; rather, the fire of nature <note>original: "Natur-feyr"</note> ignites within all things, and will melt and turn to nothing the body of every thing, or that which was tangible.

gladly reveal the <term>Tincture; in Böhme’s thought, the spiritual essence or "soul" that gives life and quality to matter</term> in its being, so that the power of the Deity might appear in it and it would be free from vanity. 22. For many are seeking now, and those who find: one finds gold, another silver, one copper, another tin. And yet this should not be understood as literal metals, but as the spirit in the power, in the great wonder of God, in the spirit of eternal power.

23. Therefore, not everything is from the Devil, as the world in <term>Babel; the author's term for the confusion and strife of competing church denominations</term> screams in its great folly, where people throw everything into one heap and want to call it a day <note>original: "Feyerabend machen"; literally to make a "quitting time" or to stop the work of spiritual inquiry</note>, putting <term>Epicureanism; here used to mean a focus on worldly pleasure and a disregard for spiritual depth</term> in its place.

Should he then throw away the whole crop or burn it for the sake of the thistles and the weeds

<margin>25.</margin>
Thus it is said to the mocker that he is a weed, and he will be thrown to the animals. And if other seeds are found among the wheat while he winnows <note>original: "worffelt"; the process of blowing air through grain to remove the husks</note> and sieves—seeds he cannot fully remove—should he then for that reason not use the wheat for his food? Yet every grain has its own power: one strengthens the heart, another the stomach, the third the limbs. For a single <term>Essence; the internal "being" or quality of a thing</term> alone does not make a <term>Tincture; the spiritual life-force or soul-spirit that gives nature its color and power</term>, but all essences together create the senses and the understanding.

<margin>26. Flowers and Herbs.</margin>
Go out into a meadow and look at the flowers and herbs, which all grow out of the earth; one herb is always more beautiful and fragrant than another, and yet often the most despised has the greatest virtue. Now the physician comes and searches: but he generally turns his <term>Mind; original: "Gemühte," the seat of one's disposition and thoughts</term> toward the largest and most beautiful herbs because they grow so vigorously and have a strong scent. He supposes they are the best, even though often a small, unsightly herb would better serve him as <term>medicine; original: "Artzeney"</term> for the patient he has in his care.

<margin>27.</margin>
Thus I give this to you to recognize: Heaven is a sower, and God gives him seed, and the elements are the field in which the seed is sown. Now Heaven has the stars, and also receives God’s seed, which sows everything mixed together. Now the essences of the stars receive the seed in the field and <term>inter-operate; original: "inqualiren," a term Böhme uses to describe how different qualities or forces interact and merge to produce a specific effect</term> with it, rising up within the herb until a seed is also formed in the herb.

<margin>29.</margin> Therefore, my dear <term>Mind; original: "Gemühte," the seat of one's disposition and thoughts</term>, watch what you do; do not judge so hastily. <margin>30.</margin> If you wish to know the difference—which is a false seed or herb (meaning a false spirit in which the pearl or the Spirit of God does not dwell)—then recognize it by its growth, its scent, and its taste. Such a person is a thistle and will be winnowed out <note>original: "außgestebet"; the process of separating dust and chaff from grain</note> by God’s Sower. Depart from such a person, for he is like a "confused wheel" <note>a Böhmean metaphor for a chaotic, restless mind lacking a divine center</note> and has no foundation. He has no sap or power from God for his growth, but grows only like a thistle that stings and bears no good seed.

1. Since in our previous writings there are several words which might be misunderstood by the reader, especially where we have written: we will be in the resurrection of the dead in the body of Jesus Christ in the <term>Holy Ternary; original Latin: "Ternario Sancto"</term>. While we have called the <term>Holy Ternary; original Latin: "Ternarium Sanctum"</term> "holy earth," it should not be understood as common soil, but rather as the holy body arising from the holy power of the <term>Trinity of God; original: "Dreyheit Gottes"</term>. In our writing, the "Holy Ternary" is actually understood as the gateways of God the Father, from whom all things proceed as if from a single essence.

Therefore, we wish to inform the reader of the second book of our writings somewhat more thoroughly, so that he does not merely cling to the bare letter and treat our writings as a <note>original: "Hiſtoriſch Weſen." Böhme warns against "historical" knowledge—meaning a literal or academic understanding that lacks personal spiritual experience.</note> historical matter; rather, he should pay attention to the sense and spirit—what is intended when the author speaks of the Divine Life. In these descriptions, the author does not use only one kind of word or name, even though sometimes three or four different names refer to exactly the same single life.

No, that is a deception; you deceive yourself.

The book of the **Three Principles** <term>original: "drey Principiis"; Böhme’s system of the three worlds: the dark world (divine wrath/fire), the light world (divine love), and the external world (our visible nature).</term> of Divine Essence, and of the Essence of all Essences, is a key and an alphabet for all those who desire to understand my writings: and it deals with the Creation: with the **Eternal Birth** <term>original: "Ewige Gebuhrt"; the ongoing process by which God reveals Himself and generates the divine life.</term> of the Godhead: with Repentance, the Justification of man, and his life in Paradise, and with the Fall: Likewise, with the New Birth and Christ’s Testaments, and with the whole of human Salvation, etc., which is very profitable to read: For it is an eye to recognize the wonders in the **Mystery of God** <note>original: "Mysterio Gottes"; the hidden depths of the divine nature and the unfolding of His plan.</note>.

### Chapter 12. §. 15.

<margin>29.</margin>
The author’s description stands upon the ground of Scripture and is nothing new; nor will it ever become anything new, except for true knowledge in the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "H. Geist"</note>, who is the Essence of all Essences.

<margin>30.</margin>
My writings are not written for the swine, who despise the **Light of Nature** <term>original: "Liecht der Natur"; a concept suggesting that God has placed a natural wisdom or "light" within the world that allows humans to understand spiritual truths through the physical creation.</term> and walk in animal ways: but for the children who are to possess the Kingdom of God. For I have written them for myself and for those who seek, and not for the clever and the wise of this world.

->Jacob Böhme, The True Author Wrote This<-
<note>original: "Jacob Böhme, V. A. S."; the initials V. A. S. likely stand for the Latin "Verus Auctor Scripsit."</note>
